Tutorial & Guide

Guide level: Everyday steps for each of the 4 tools, plus how to export & install.

What this tool is

One offline app for building DOOM: The Dark Ages mods. It has four tools — Texture Tool (reskin the Slayer, weapons and demons), Weapon Stats (damage, fire rate, ammo, range), HUD Sprite (the Doomguy face) and Model Swap (give a weapon a different model). You can use any combination in a single mod.

1 · Start a mod

  1. On launch you get the start screen. Give the mod a name (leave it blank and it’s called Untitled), tick which tools it uses, then press Create.
  2. Optionally narrow it to certain categories (Slayer only, say) — the other tabs are hidden and a ＋ chip appears on the tab strip to bring them back.
  3. Already made something? Load opens an existing mod folder — you can also drag a folder straight onto the Load button.
  4. Prefer to poke about first? Skip. Nothing is created until you say so.

Each launch starts with no project open — the bar reads Current project: None until you create or open one. Reloading with F8 keeps whatever you have open.

2 · The top bar

  • Create / Load — start a new mod, or open one.
  • Current project — the mod’s name and its menu: Save, Export, Rename, a random name, Edit tools & categories, and your Recent mods.
  • Settings — appearance, sound, modding options and folder locations.
  • The three tool buttons on the right. The ＋ beside them adds a tool; once all three are in it becomes a − — click it either way to tick or untick tools.
  • The colours follow whichever tool you’re in: the Texture Tool takes the current tab’s colour, Weapon Stats is purple, HUD Sprite is green.

3 · Two ways to skin a part

  • Standard PNG — drop your own image onto a part. The glow sliders control how much it glows in-game.
  • Transparency + Animation — select a part, then drag Opacity to make it see-through, glowing and animated instead of painting it. Brightness, Speed and Animation are set with the other sliders.

The box on the right of those sliders shows what you are editing. Click a section (say Body Armour) or a single part to select it — the sliders then change only that, and rows showing its own value get an own badge. With nothing selected you’re editing the defaults every transparent part falls back to. Click the same thing again to deselect.

4 · Doing a whole section or tab at once

  • Section controls (on each section) — make that section transparent, or recolour it.
  • Category controls (right of the tab bar) — the same for the entire tab.
  • Both open a small menu; Recolour reveals a colour picker with a hex box you can paste into.

5 · Checking what you’ve done

Click the parts assigned pill. It asks what you want to see — textures applied, transparency & animation, PBR layers (advanced), weapon stats — then lists just that.

6 · Export → Package → Load

  1. Export mod folder writes a <name>_Source folder.
  2. 📦 Package hands it to FlavorfulGecko5’s Atlan Mod Packager, which turns it into a game-ready zip.
  3. ▶ Load & Launch runs the Atlan Mod Loader and starts the game.

Both Atlan tools must live inside your DOOM: The Dark Ages folder. Set their locations under Settings ▸ Folders & locations.

Handy to know

  • F2 toggles Advanced textures (per-part PBR channels). F8 reloads the tool.
  • Settings ▸ Master Sound silences everything — music, the startup sting and UI sounds.
  • Settings ▸ Write .decl files (advanced) exports texture aliases only. Use it when you’re building on a kit that ships its own declarations. Warning: glow, transparency, eyes and hair are produced by those files and stop working while it’s off.
  • Every popup with just an OK can be silenced for the session via Don’t show this again.

1 · Add your textures

  1. In the PNG Tray on the left, click Add PNGs and pick one or more PNG images. These are your camo / skin textures.
  2. Or open SirBiggieCheese Preset Camos and drag any camo onto a part, a Fill box, or the tray — or click Add all camos to PNG Tray to add every one.

2 · Assign textures to parts

  1. Pick a tab (Slayer, Weapons, Demons…). Each card is a part of the game.
  2. Drag a PNG from the tray onto a part, or click the part to browse for one.
  3. Drag a PNG Here to Fill Current Tab paints every part on that tab at once.
  4. Randomize buttons scatter tray textures across the current tab, or everything.
  5. Use the search box at the top to find a part by name across every tab.

3 · Fine control (optional)

  • Click the “targets” line on a part to see the exact game texture paths, and assign a different PNG to each one.
  • Drop a texture on a section’s Drag PNG Here to Fill Section box to skin that whole section at once.
  • The Glow sliders set how brightly each category emits light (0 = matte, 20 = furnace). The switch turns glow off entirely.
Want glowing, see-through parts, per-part PBR channels, or a different Slayer/Shield skin? Those live in the Advanced guide — switch Guide level to Advanced at the top.

4 · Export

  1. Type a mod name (or hit New name), then click Export Mod Folder.
  2. First time only: it asks for your default export folder. Make a fresh folder such as DTDA Mod Packs and pick it — every export goes there automatically after that (so you never hunt for it). You can put it anywhere; Shift-click Export to change it later.
  3. The tool writes <name>_Source into that folder (your PNGs + a darkagesmod.txt).
  4. That folder is not the finished mod yet — see the New to Modding? tab to package and install it.
Then use the buttons under Export — always in this order:
  1. Export mod folder — writes your _Source folder wherever you choose.
  2. Package — opens the Atlan Packager so you can package that folder into your mods folder. (Locked until you’ve exported.)
  3. Load — runs the Atlan Mod Loader and launches the game.
Tip: Load Existing Mod Folder re-imports a _Source folder you exported earlier, so you can tweak a skin instead of rebuilding it.
Keep track of your work: after every export, a small “Last exported” note appears under the mod-name box showing the mod’s name and the exact folder it was written to. It stays there between sessions, so you always know what you built last and where it went — every tool (Texture, Weapon Stat Editor, HUD Sprite) shows its own.

What this tab does

The Weapon Stat Editor tweaks your weapons across several stats: Damage, Fire Rate, Ammo Capacity and Range (each in its own collapsible section, every weapon listed A–Z). Every weapon gets a slider per stat, running from 0 to 10 in 0.1 steps — drag it and that weapon does that many times its normal value (1.0× = vanilla, 2.0× = double, 0.5× = half, 10× = one-shot most things). Damage and Fire Rate are confirmed working in-game; Ammo and Range carry a Test badge until confirmed.

Each section heading carries a Set all slider that moves every weapon in that section at once, a 🎲 to randomise them, and a ↺ to put the whole section back to vanilla. The ↺ on a card resets just that weapon.

▸ Quick start (beginner)

  1. Open Weapon Stats at the top.
  2. Open a section — Weapon Damage, Fire Rate, Ammo Capacity or Range — and find your weapon (they are A–Z).
  3. Drag its slider. The label shows the live multiplier, e.g. “4.0×”, and the card lights up as changed.
  4. Type a mod name (or hit New name) → Export → Package → Load — same three-step flow as the texture tool.
  5. Only weapons whose slider you moved are written into the mod. Leave a slider at 1.0× and that weapon is untouched.
Undo: the ↶ Undo button (and Ctrl+Z) steps back your slider changes. Clear all resets every weapon to 1.0×.
Advanced — how it works & what to watch for
  • What a multiplier actually scales. Each weapon’s damage lives across several game decls (a base decl plus _choke/_cylindrical/_splash/firemode variants) and in more than one field: pointBlankDamage, the object max/minDamage, and bare per-enemy maxDamage caps. The tool multiplies all of those and leaves damageScalar alone, so you get a clean ×N with no double-scaling. (Early versions only touched one field, which is why cranking a weapon used to do nothing.)
  • Split weapons. Some in-game weapons share one physical weapon but fire two ways, so they appear as two sliders: Accelerator / Plasma Rifle, Impaler / Shredder (harpoon vs. blackjack), Ravager / Skull Crusher (choke vs. base). Tune them independently.
  • Naming. Crossbow is the in-tool name for the weapon whose decls are still called bfg/PLAYER_WEAPON_BFG internally — that’s expected, not a bug.
  • Chain Shot has no damage slider of its own — on purpose. Checked against the extracted game: there is no damage/firearm/striker* decl at all. aidamagedeclcollection/slayer/weapon_reanimator_striker points the Chain Shot at damage/firearm/reanimator_orb_* — the same files the Reanimator uses. That is why the damage card is labelled Reanimator / Chain Shot: one slider, because the game gives them one set of files. Two sliders would just fight each other over the same text. It does have its own Fire Rate and Ammo, which is why it appears in those sections.
  • Sections do not all hold the same weapons. That is the game, not a missing feature, and each section says why underneath its heading. Range only lists weapons that fire a projectile with a maxRange, so hitscan weapons (Chain Shot, Crossbow, Plasma Rifle) are absent.
  • Two extra sections appear in dev mode (F4): Projectile Speed and Move Speed While Firing. Both are unproven — they carry the Test badge for a reason.
  • Melee weapons are not here. Flail / mace / spear / shield use a separate damage/damage/melee/ decl family that hasn’t been validated with the scaler, so they’re intentionally left out for now.
  • It’s a text mod. Damage decls are plain text (loadPriority 100), so this export needs no Atlan Packager image conversion — but you still Package/Load through Atlan so it lands in mods\. A damage mod and a texture mod are different types and coexist fine.
Balance tip: start at 1.5×–2× for a “stronger but still fun” run; 5×+ trivialises most fights and 10× one-shots bosses. There’s no upside to going past what one-shots — extra multiplier is wasted.

What this tab does

The HUD Sprite Editor replaces the little Doom-guy face (and related HUD sprites) at the bottom of your screen with your own art. You drop in a sprite sheet — a grid of small face images — and the tool ships it as a HUD texture mod.

▸ Quick start (beginner)

  1. Open HUD Sprite at the top.
  2. Drop your sprite sheet onto the drop zone — or take one from the preset strips on the left, either by clicking it or by dragging it onto the drop zone.
  3. Haven’t got a sheet? Press AI prompt in the bar. It opens a ready-written description of this exact layout — fill in your character, copy it, and paste it into any AI image generator.
  4. The sheet is an 11 columns × 5 rows grid on a transparent background, no gridlines. Rows = health bands (full → near-death); columns = facing/expression. If you just want a quick swap, a single repeated face across the grid works fine.
  5. Name it → Export → Package → Load. The export name is DTDA-HUD-Sprite-<###>.
  6. Launch and take damage — the face reacts to your health just like vanilla.
⚠ The one rule that makes it package: ship one HUD texture at a time (the default main face). The zombie / hologram extras are OFF by default — leave them off unless you need them. See the advanced note below for why.
Advanced — the grid, the packaging trap & extras
  • The atlas. The original face texture is 1496×815, an 11×5 grid of 136×163 cells on transparent background. Cols 1–8 are facing/expression, cols 9–10 are the yellow-eye buff/powerup faces (easy to forget), col 11 is the severe-damage face; each row is a health band. Your sheet doesn’t have to be exactly 1496×815 — the preview computes cells from the actual image size (width/11 × height/5) — but keeping the 11×5 proportions keeps faces aligned in-game.
  • ⚠ Why extras are off by default (the packaging trap). HUD faces are bc7 textures, and the Atlan Mod Packager crashes when it GPU-encodes more than one bc7 UI texture in a single package (confirmed with the packager’s author). So a default export ships exactly one UI texture (the main face) and packages cleanly. If you enable the zombie/hologram extras you’ll get a warning — you can still do it, but you may have to package them as separate mods.
  • Presets are small square tiles drawn from cell (0,0) of the actual sheet, centred — a fast way to preview a look without loading a full sheet. Every tile is draggable onto the drop zone. Your Presets is your own list: Save current sheet adds the sheet you have loaded, Add your own preset takes PNGs straight off disk, and right-clicking a tile deletes it.
  • Adding to the built-in preset list (dev mode). With F4 dev mode on, a ＋ Add sheet to presets button appears under the top strip. Sheets added there sit alongside the shipped ones, marked with a dashed outline, and right-click removes them. They are stored on this machine only. ⤓ Save added sheets writes them out as real PNGs — move those into presets\faces\ and they are picked up automatically from then on.
  • It’s a real texture mod (needs the Atlan Packager to convert PNG → bc7), unlike the text-only damage and transparency mods. If packaging fails, check …\DOOMTheDarkAges\packager_log.txt — a bc7 GPU-encode crash there almost always means “too many UI textures at once.”
Drawing your own sheet: transparent background, no gridlines, all 11 columns (don’t forget the two buff/powerup columns), 5 health-band rows. A green-tinted copy of the same grid makes the optional zombie sheet.

What this tab does

Model Swap gives a weapon a different model from the ones the game already ships. The Skull Crusher can hold the Crucible; the Mace can be the Crucible; the Flail can be the Chainsaw. Nothing is imported — you are pointing a weapon at a shape that is already in the game.

▸ Quick start

  1. Open Model Swap at the top.
  2. Find a weapon card and pick a model from its dropdown. Options marked (tested) are confirmed working in game.
  3. Press the 🎲 dice on a section to fill it in with tested models only.
  4. Name it → Export → Package → Load.
One card can change two weapons. Cards are named for the model, not the weapon — “Skull Crusher / Ravager” means both weapons share one model and both will change. The card name always tells you what is affected.
Advanced — which models work, and why
  • Options marked (tested) are proven in game. Everything else in the dropdown is available to try but unconfirmed — most swaps crash the game, so treat an untested pick as an experiment and load it on its own.
  • The dice only rolls tested models, so a random fill can never build a mod that crashes.
  • Why most models fail. A weapon’s animations move named bones. Give it a shape whose skeleton has different bones and the game has nothing to move, so it crashes on load. The models that work are the ones whose skeletons happen to suit.
  • Melee weapons have more choices. The Mace, Flail, Shield and Spear are edited a different way internally, which unlocks a longer list for those cards.
  • Animations stay with the original weapon. A swapped model may reload or swing oddly — that is inherent to swapping, not a fault in the export.
  • It stacks with the Texture Tool. Model Swap and texture mods touch different files, so a reshaped weapon can be reskinned too.

What this tab does

The AI Health Editor changes how much health every enemy has. Enemies are grouped by kind — Fodder, Heavy, Super Heavy and so on, taken from the game’s own ai/<class>/ folders — and listed A–Z inside each group. Drag a slider and the new health is shown right beside it, so you can watch a Hell Knight go from 12,000 to 24,000 before you export anything.

▸ Quick start (beginner)

  1. Nothing to set up — the enemy files ship with the app. If a bar says some are missing, press Add folder and point it at a game extract made with remove_binary_files = 0.
  2. Find your enemy. The search box filters every group at once.
  3. Drag its slider. 1.0× is vanilla; the number next to it is the health you will actually get.
  4. Use Set all in a group heading to move a whole class at once — e.g. every Fodder enemy to 0.5× for a faster, squishier run.
  5. Name it → Export → Package → Load, the same three steps as every other tool. Only enemies you actually changed are written into the mod.
Advanced — how it works & what to watch for
  • How the patch works. Health is a float32 that appears exactly twice in an enemy’s compiled file — once as max and once as starting. The tool overwrites those four bytes in place. The file stays exactly the same length, so nothing shifts and the round trip is byte-for-byte identical apart from the number you changed.
  • What gets exported. The patched .bin, plus a readable .decl twin in a noload/ folder. The loader ignores noload/ entirely — it is there so your mod is legible and shareable, exactly like the two reference mods ship it.
  • ⚠ Not yet confirmed in-game. Nothing this tool builds has been loaded into DOOM yet. The one unknown is whether the compiled file carries a checksum; it is a same-length edit so probably not, but that is untested. Try one enemy first.
  • Why a text decl will not do. Exporting enemy health as a plain text decl crashes the game — confirmed twice. The patched .bin plus noload/ is the method that works.
Balance tip: raising health makes fights longer, not harder — past about 3× most encounters just become spongy. Lowering Fodder to 0.5× while raising Super Heavy is usually a better-feeling change than raising everything.

What you need

  • DOOM: The Dark Ages installed (Steam).
  • Atlan Mod Loader — makes the game load mods.
  • Atlan Mod Packager — turns your exported folder into a mod the game can read.

Both Atlan tools are community tools. Get them from Nexus Mods → DOOM: The Dark Ages (search “Atlan”). They are not bundled with this app.

1 · Find your game folder

Usually:

C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\DOOMTheDarkAges

In Steam you can also right-click the game → Manage → Browse local files.

Inside that folder, make sure there is a folder named mods. If there isn’t, create one.

2 · Build your skin

Use this tool (see the Using the Texture Tool tab) and click Export Mod Folder. You now have a folder called <name>_Source.

3 · Package it

  1. Open AtlanModPackager.exe.
  2. Point it at your <name>_Source folder.
  3. It produces a packaged .zip. This step is required because the game cannot read raw PNGs — the packager converts them to the game’s texture format.

4 · Install it

  1. Copy that packaged .zip into the game’s mods\ folder.
  2. Run AtlanModLoader.exe once. It patches the game to load whatever is in mods\.
  3. Launch DOOM: The Dark Ages and look at your gear.

5 · Removing or swapping a skin

Delete the mod’s .zip from mods\ and relaunch. To swap skins, take the old zip out first.

Important: only run one skin mod at a time for the same thing. Two mods that both retexture the Slayer will fight each other, and only one will win.
If the game updates and mods stop loading, re-run the Atlan Mod Loader. Game patches usually undo it.

PBR / CHANNELS

What is PBR? (start here)

A game surface isn’t one image — it’s a small stack of images that answer different questions about the material: What colour is it? Is it bumpy? Is it shiny or dull? Does it glow? The stack together is called PBR (Physically Based Rendering). The game combines them live with the scene lighting, which is why a good skin looks like it belongs in the world instead of a sticker slapped on top.

The one thing to remember: if you replace only the colour, the weapon still reflects light using the original shine and bump maps. That’s the “why does my skin look flat / plasticky / stuck-on?” problem. Fix it by supplying the other maps too — but you only need the ones you actually want to change.

The channels — what each one does

  • Albedo (base colour) — the flat colour and pattern, with no shadows or shine painted in. This is the main PNG you drop on a card. 90% of skins are just this.
  • Normal _n — fakes bumps, panel lines and scratches by tilting how light hits the surface. It looks purple/blue because it stores a direction, not a colour. Leave it alone unless you know what you’re doing — never recolour it.
  • Smoothness / Roughness _s / _g — how polished the surface is. White = wet/mirror gloss, black = dry/matte. Grey in between. This is the single biggest lever for “metal vs rubber vs cloth”.
  • Specular — how much light bounces off and what tint it has. Controls the metal-vs-non-metal feel alongside smoothness.
  • Emissive / Glow _e — the parts that light up on their own: runes, energy cells, vents. Black = no glow, bright = furnace. The Glow sliders in the tool drive this without needing an image.

So what do I actually need to do?

  • Just want a recolour / camo? Drop one PNG (albedo) on the part. Done. Ignore the rest.
  • Skin looks too shiny or too dull? Add a smoothness map: a mostly-dark image makes it matte, a bright one makes it glossy.
  • Want glowing bits? Nudge the Glow slider for that category, or drop an emissive map where only the glowing parts are bright and everything else is black.
  • Want it to look worn/scratched? That’s the normal map — advanced; usually best left vanilla.

PBR-only exports (no repaint needed)

You do not need a full albedo. Click a part’s “targets” line to expand its channels and assign just a smoothness, specular or emissive — only the channel(s) you supply get overridden, everything else stays vanilla. This lets you make a stock weapon glossier, or add glow, without changing its colour at all.

Rule of thumb: Albedo = colour, Smoothness = shine, Emissive = glow, Normal = bumps (leave it). Change only what you need.

Advanced mode & the Slayer Kit (reference previews)

Turn on Settings → Advanced Texture Options to unlock a PBR ▾ button on every part. It opens a little panel with one slot per channel — Albedo, Specular, Smoothness, Emissive and Normal — each with a plain-English hint of what to draw. Drop a PNG on any single slot to override just that channel; everything else stays vanilla.

When you enable advanced mode it asks whether you have Kuddly Kraken’s DOOM Slayer Skin Maker KIT. If you link its folder, each Slayer part’s panel shows a small “now” preview of the game’s current colour / shine / metal / glow map — so you can see exactly what you’re replacing before you paint over it. (Credit for the Slayer texture kit: Kuddly Kraken.)

What to draw for each slot: Albedo = your colour/pattern. Smoothness = black-and-white, white = glossy, black = matte. Specular = dark grey, brighter = more metallic. Emissive = mostly black, bright only where it should glow. All the same size/shape as the albedo.

PBR Material Presets (save once, reuse everywhere)

In advanced mode a PBR Material Presets panel appears in the left sidebar. Drop layers into its four slots (Albedo / Specular / Smooth / Glow), name it, and Save — that whole material becomes a draggable chip. Then just drag the chip onto a part’s PBR ▾ button and every layer of the material is applied to that part in one go (drop it onto a single PBR slot to apply just that one layer). This is how you reuse a “chrome” or “gold” look across many parts without redoing the work.

Glow brightness: each part’s PBR panel has an Emissive / Bloom brightness slider — it sets how bright that part’s glow layer shines (0 = off). If you added an Emissive map, this controls how strongly it lights up.

SLAYER & SHIELD SKINS (SETS)

Skinning a specific in-game skin

The Slayer (and their shield) has many in-game skins — Default, Nightmare, Ranger, Executioner, Divinity, and more. With Advanced Texture Options ON, a collapsible “Slayer skin:” picker appears at the top of the Slayer tab, and a “Shield skin:” picker on the Melee Weapons tab.

  • Pick a skin from the list — the tab then shows that skin’s parts, so your PNGs target that skin only. Default is the base Slayer (what most people mod).
  • Each skin’s parts are independent, so you can build a mod for one skin without touching the others.
  • The pickers are hidden unless Advanced Texture Options is on, so normal users just edit the main skin.
Note: Eyes and hair are hidden — they use special game materials a plain PNG can’t skin, so they don’t work yet. Skin, cape and visor glass do work and are kept.

TRANSPARENCY / GHOST MODE (confirmed working in-game)

  • Click Transparency / Animation (next to Standard PNG mode) at the top. The app always opens in Standard PNG mode — Transparency is opt-in each time.
  • It’s an on/off toggle per part. Each part shows a Clear tick box (above its label) with its own colour swatch — a checkerboard means no colour chosen yet. Tick the parts to make see-through and pick a colour.
  • Use Make this category transparent/section to make many parts transparent at once, and 🎨 Recolour to apply one colour. A part’s own swatch overrides the group colour. A fully transparent section glows white (like a full PNG fill glows green).
  • The panel sliders tune the whole look: Opacity (see-through), Glow (brightness), Speed and Pattern (Smoke / Drift / Swirl / Streaks / Static).
  • A see-through part won’t take a PNG — that’s why its PNG area greys out. To undo it, switch to Standard PNG and untick See-through on that part.
  • Export as normal — transparent parts render see-through, tinted and animated; PNG parts export as usual. You can mix both in one mod.

HOW THE TOOL WORKS

How the tool is built (developer reference)

What this tool actually is

It’s a self-contained desktop app for building DOOM: The Dark Ages texture/camo mods. You assign PNG images to specific in-game materials (“targets”), optionally tweak glow/PBR, and it writes out a mod-source folder the community Atlan tools turn into something the game loads.

What it’s built with

  • One big HTML file (index.html) — the entire interface, styling and logic live here: HTML for structure, CSS for the look, and plain JavaScript (no framework, no build step) for everything it does.
  • Electron shell (the SkinBuilder-App folder) — Electron is Chromium + Node.js wrapped as a native window, so the same web page runs as a real Windows app with file access. Node is what lets it read/write folders and zip files, which a normal browser can’t.
  • A few data files loaded alongside it (data/enemies_data.js, data/atlan_data.js, data/env_data.js, data/vanilla_pbr.js) — these are just big lists of the game’s material paths, grouped into the tabs and cards you see.

How it’s structured (top to bottom of the file)

  • <style> — the whole visual theme (dark/red DOOM look, per-tab accent colours, the glass panels).
  • <body> — the top toolbar (Edit / Settings / Tutorial / music / nav), the PNG tray, the tab bar, and the grid of target cards.
  • One large inline <script> — builds the cards from the data lists, handles drag-and-drop, glow sliders, presets, search, randomize, and the exporter.
  • Popup templates at the very end for the extra windows.

Targets, cards and “decls”

Every card maps to one or more target paths — the exact address of a material inside the game, e.g. art/weapons/shield/…. When you export, the tool writes a small text decl (declaration) for each assigned target telling the game “use this image for that material’s colour / normal / smoothness / emissive”, plus a darkagesmod.txt that registers the whole thing. Channels you don’t touch are left as vanilla.

What happens when you click Export

  1. The tool gathers every assigned PNG + its target(s).
  2. It writes a <name>_Source folder: your images, the generated decls, and the mod manifest.
  3. You run that folder through the Atlan Packager — that’s the step that converts raw PNGs into the game’s real texture format (the game can’t read PNGs directly).
  4. The Atlan Loader patches the game to read the mods\ folder, and you play.

The Atlan Packager and Loader are made by FlavorfulGecko5 (download separately). Keep both inside your DOOM: The Dark Ages game folder — they only work from there.

Where your settings live

Your preferences (startup sound, music autoplay + volume, monochrome UI, ticked presets, text edits) are saved in the app’s local storage on your machine, so they survive a restart. Nothing is uploaded anywhere — the tool is fully offline.

Two kinds of skins

  • Texture skins (what this tool mainly does) — new images on existing materials. Needs the Atlan Packager.
  • Text-only / effect mods — some effects (like glow or transparency recipes) are done purely by editing material decls that reuse the game’s own built-in textures, so they need no custom images and no packager — they can ship as a plain drag-and-drop zip.
TL;DR: a single HTML/CSS/JavaScript page, run as a desktop app via Electron/Node, that turns your PNGs + a list of game material paths into Atlan-ready mod files. Everything is local and offline.
Full reference: HowTheToolWorks.txt in the tool folder.

Exports a ready-to-package mod (raw PNGs + aliasing, same as the Mugshot Template). By default it ships just the main hud_face_classic face — one bc7 UI texture, which the Atlan Packager handles cleanly. The zombie/hologram variants are optional extras (each is another UI texture the current packager can't encode alongside others yet).
